content:
My honest answer: I wouldn't go next spring. And I want to be clear that's not me picking your family over your dream — I think the timing is what's wrong, not the dream.

Start with the actual risk. Without oxygen on an 8000er, the danger isn't abstract. Attempting these peaks without O2 multiplies your death risk several-fold compared with using it, and on some mountains a no-O2 attempt carries a real chance — a few percent, sometimes worse — of dying, with frostbite amputations and cerebral edema more likely than death itself. And if you get into trouble, the people sent into the death zone after you are usually Sherpas. None of this is disqualifying on its own. Adults are allowed to take big risks. The question is proportion, and you have a six-year-old and a nine-year-old.

Here's where I'd push back on your own framing, though: "now or never" is false. In eight years your youngest is 14 and you're 49. That's not too old — Ed Viesturs finished climbing all fourteen 8000ers *without oxygen* at 49. The mountain will still be there. The one thing that won't still be there is your children's childhood — the years when they can't yet understand the dream but would fully inherit the loss.

I'm also not pretending staying is free. A parent who amputates a dream doesn't become a better father — he becomes a quieter one, and the resentment shows up at dinner. So don't amputate it. Reschedule it. Keep training. Pick the year, write it down with your wife, and between now and then climb something serious — an 8000er with oxygen, or a hard 7000er without it. That feeds the dream *and* makes the eventual no-O2 attempt genuinely safer rather than just postponed. This matters especially if the peak you have in mind is one of the killers — Annapurna, K2, Kangchenjunga — and softens somewhat if it's Cho Oyu. Be honest with yourself about which conversation you're actually having.

One more thing. You said part of you agrees with your wife. Listen to that part. The dreaming part of you has never been asked to do the risk math — that's what makes it a dream. And the difference between a climb your wife merely endures and one she eventually stands behind, even grudgingly, is the difference between a story your family tells and a wound it keeps reopening.

The dream isn't childish, and wanting it at 41 with two kids is allowed. But dreams take their meaning from the life around them. Give it eight years and it can still become something you did — instead of something your family lost you to.
reasoning:
The user is asking a deeply personal, high-stakes life question: whether to attempt an 8000m peak without supplemental oxygen next spring, while having young kids (6 and 9). They explicitly asked for my honest opinion, not a pros-and-cons table. They want a genuine perspective.

Let me think about this carefully. This is a request for personal advice on a genuinely difficult question. The person has trained for years, it's "the dream of my life," but their wife opposes it and part of them agrees with her. They're 41, kids 6 and 9.

What do I actually think about this? Let me reason through the substance first, then think about form.

**The substance:**

First, let me be honest about the actual risk profile. 8000m peaks without supplemental oxygen. The death rate on 8000ers is significant — historically around 3-5% overall for all climbers, but without oxygen it's considerably higher. On some mountains (K2, Annapurna, Kangchenjunga), no-O2 attempts have death rates in the double digits historically. Even the "safer" 8000ers like Cho Oyu, Manaslu, Shishapangma without O2 carry substantial mortality risk. Plus, death isn't the only bad outcome: amputations (frostbite), HACE/HAPE, cerebral edema causing permanent damage, becoming a burden on Sherpas who may die trying to rescue you (this is a real moral consideration — your rescue may kill others).

The person says "an 8000-metre peak" — they didn't specify which one. If it's Cho Oyu, that's one thing; if it's K2 without oxygen, that's another. I might note that the specific mountain matters enormously. Actually, that's a useful point: the risk is not uniform. A no-O2 attempt on Cho Oyu via normal route is very different from K2 in winter or Annapurna. If they haven't picked, or if they have, this matters.

Second, the framing "do I have the right" is interesting. The wife frames it as rights. But there's a philosophical debate here: parents take risks all the time (driving, etc.). The question is proportionality. Driving to work carries maybe 1-in-8,000 annual death risk in some countries. A no-O2 8000er attempt carries perhaps 1-in-30 to 1-in-100 death risk per expedition depending on the mountain, plus serious injury risk of similar or greater magnitude. So it's orders of magnitude above ordinary parental risk. The "rights" framing can obscure that this isn't about whether parents may ever take risks; it's about whether this specific risk is proportionate.

Third, the dream of a lifetime. This is real. People who abandon core dreams sometimes carry regret that poisons their family life. But dreams can also be revised rather than abandoned. There are intermediate options: oxygen-assisted ascent (still a massive achievement, far safer), a different peak, waiting until kids are older (the 6-year-old will be 14; the 9-year-old 17 — the intensive parenting years are finite, roughly 8-10 more years). Waiting isn't the same as never. At 41, he's not old for high-altitude mountaineering — many climbers do their best no-O2 work in their late 40s and 50s (e.g., many Sherpas climb no-O2 into their 40s-50s; notable Western no-O2 climbers have been in their 40s-50s). Physiologically, VO2max declines slowly; with continued training, a 48-50-year-old can still do this. So "now or never" is factually questionable, and that's a key point: the frame of the dilemma (now vs. never) may be false. It's now vs. later, and later is actually viable.

Fourth, the wife. The user says "My wife says I have no right to take that risk... and honestly part of me agrees." So he's not fully committed to going; he's torn. The wife's opposition matters not just as a constraint but as information. A marriage where one partner undertakes a mission the other believes is wrong, potentially leaving her a single parent — that has costs even if he survives. And the kids: a 6- and 9-year-old don't understand "dream"; they understand dad might not come home. Though kids are also resilient and a parent modeling courage matters... but the courage model only works if the parent comes home or if the story is bearable. The counterfactual — kids losing a parent to a chosen risk during childhood — is one of the most damaging things that can happen to them. The research on parental bereavement is sobering: elevated risks of depression, anxiety, worse outcomes. That's not decisive by itself but it's real.

Fifth, what does "what you really think" invite? He explicitly doesn't want a wishy-washy both-sides answer. He wants me to actually take a position. I should do that. I think honesty here means: if I had to bet, I'd lean toward... what?

Let me actually form a view. My honest view: I would not go this spring, and I don't think this is moral cowardice or a failure to respect the dream. Reasons:

1. The risk math without oxygen on an 8000er is not a "small chance of dying" — it's a material chance of death or life-altering injury, plausibly in the few-percent-to-tens-of-percent range depending on mountain and conditions. With kids at 6 and 9, the expected cost is enormous and falls on people who didn't choose it.

2. The timing asymmetry: the kids' childhood is a window; the mountain isn't going anywhere. In 8 years he's 49 — still viable for no-O2 8000m (rare but real; he'd have years to keep training, acclimatize experience, choose a good window, maybe pick a more moderate 8000er). Waiting converts a coin-flip against his family's wishes into a possible yes later that everyone can live with — possibly even with his wife's eventual buy-in, which changes everything about how the climb is done and how it would be remembered.

3. The dream framing "next spring" as the deadline is manufactured. Unless there's something I don't know (a specific reason next spring is unique), the urgency is psychological, not real.

4. However — and this is important for honesty — I should not pretend the stay-home option is costless. He may carry real grief. The answer isn't "the dream is silly"; it's "the dream survives a delay; a child's one childhood doesn't survive his death." Also, there are meaningful interim things: climb a 7000er or an 8000er with oxygen to build experience, keep the no-O2 dream alive as the capstone for later, involve the family, maybe get the wife genuinely on board (her opposition now isn't just an obstacle; a climb done over her objections is haunted either way — if something happens, she lives with "I told him"; if nothing happens, trust may still be damaged).

5. There's also the Sherpa/teammate dimension: no-O2 attempts raise the chance you need a rescue that endangers others. That's worth one line, not a lecture.

6. One more consideration: "part of me agrees" — I should take that seriously. People asking "tell me what you really think" often already sense the answer and want permission or a push. But I should not just tell him what he wants to hear either. I genuinely do think staying this spring is the right call on the merits, and I can say that with conviction while honoring the dream.

Wait — let me steelman going. Someone who says "go" would argue: (a) A parent who shows up hollow, having amputated their dream, is not fully present; the resentment leaks. (b) Life is risky; you could die crossing the street; living in fear is not living. (c) The wife knew who she married (though — the dream may predate kids, we don't know). (d) Four weeks away is a bounded absence; and modern 8000er climbing with logistics is far safer than in the 80s-90s (weather forecasts, helicopters on some peaks, better meds, pre-acclimatization). (e) Kids benefit from a parent who is alive to himself.

How much do I concede? (a) is real but there's a difference between deferring a dream and amputating it; I'm proposing deferral with a concrete plan, which addresses the resentment risk. (b) the street-crossing analogy fails on magnitude — you don't take on 1-5% death risk recreationally. (d) true but no-O2 specifically remains the great risk multiplier; improved logistics reduce but don't flatten it. (e) the "alive to himself" point is best honored by keeping the dream alive with a plan, not by pressing the go button against his own doubts and his wife's.

So my actual position: don't go this spring; reframe the goal as no-O2 8000m when the kids are older, with a family plan, and consider intermediate summits with oxygen in the meantime to keep momentum and build competence. Also, decide the specific mountain matters; some no-O2 objectives are categorically more lethal.

I should be careful about one thing: I shouldn't be preachy or moralize excessively. He asked for my real opinion. I'll give it plainly, then justify it in a human way, then sketch what "staying" should mean so it doesn't read as surrender. And I should acknowledge the legitimacy of the ache — that the person who wants to go is not a bad father for wanting it. The desire is not shameful; the timing is the problem.

Also, should I ask clarifying questions (which mountain? has he discussed a timeline with his wife?) — he asked for an opinion, not an intake interview. I can note the mountain matters in one line without demanding info. The response should be mostly the opinion, delivered directly, in prose, no tables, no headers probably — a personal letter-like response fits the register. Medium length. Not a wall of bullet points. This is a human moment; formatting should be minimal, conversational prose. Maybe 300-450 words. He asked "tell me what you really think" — so the first thing should be the actual answer, not throat-clearing.

Let me also be careful with the risk figures. Rough honest numbers: no-O2 ascents are a minority of 8000er summits; death rates for no-O2 climbers are several times higher than with-O2. For example, on Everest, no-O2 climbers historically had death rates around 5-8% (some analyses show ~5-6% no-O2 vs ~1% with O2 in modern era). On Annapurna, overall death rate historically ~30% summit-to-death ratio, much lower now. I should avoid fake precision. I can say "roughly, depending on the mountain, a no-O2 attempt carries something like a 1-in-20 to 1-in-50 chance of death, and comparable odds of losing fingers or worse" — hmm, is that defensible? For no-O2 attempts across 8000ers, published mortality for no-O2 summiteers/attempters varies widely: Cho Oyu no-O2 is relatively safer, Annapurna/K2 no-O2 much worse. A defensible statement: "on most 8000ers, climbing without oxygen multiplies your death risk several-fold compared with using it, and for the harder mountains the risk for a no-O2 attempt is in the few-percent range, sometimes worse." That's honest without fake precision. I could also mention that serious injury (frostbite amputations, HACE) is more likely than death. Good.

Also worth naming: the wife's phrase "no right" is legally wrong but morally pointed — the real question is whether this risk is proportionate to what your absence would cost if it went wrong, and only you and she can price that, but with kids at 6 and 9, the price is very high. I think the strongest single line: the mountain will still be there when your daughter is 14 (or the younger one is 14). Your children's childhood will not. At 49-50 you can still do this without oxygen — that's not sentiment, that's physiology; the record of no-O2 climbers shows 40s-50s are viable. So the choice isn't dream vs. kids; it's dream now with a loaded gun vs. dream in 8 years with your wife possibly standing behind you instead of against you.

One more nuance: he says "part of me agrees" with the wife. I want to honor that part. The honest read is that his gut already knows. People rarely write to an AI for a pros/cons table when they already have one; they write when the heart and the gut disagree. I can say: the part of you that agrees with her is worth listening to, not because the dream is wrong, but because it already knows what the timing costs.

I should also give the "go" case its due in a sentence or two so he sees I've considered it, not strawmanned it. Something like: the case for going is real — a parent who kills his dream often doesn't become a better father, he becomes a quieter one, and the resentment shows up at dinner. But there's a difference between killing a dream and rescheduling it.

And concretely what to do: 
- Keep training; pick the objective and a target year (e.g., when the youngest is ~14).
- Consider an intermediate: 8000er with oxygen or a 7000er no-O2 as a stepping stone — keeps the dream fed and makes the later attempt safer.
- Do the marriage work: get her from "I forbid it" to "I hate it but I'm in" — a climb she consents to changes the moral weather entirely. Also practical: wills, insurance (check mountaineering exclusions), etc. Maybe too much logistics; keep light.
- Note the rescue-others point briefly.

Also: I might ask, rhetorically, which mountain — because if it's K2 without O2 in spring... actually spring K2 is unusual (K2 attempts are usually summer); "next spring" suggests maybe an Everest north side, Cho Oyu (closed to foreigners recently, actually Tibet permits were closed for years — reopening was announced for 2025?), Lhotse, Makalu, Shishapangma... I shouldn't over-index on permit politics. I'll just say the specific mountain changes the math a lot, and if it's one of the deadly ones, even more so.

Hmm, also — should I worry this is a suicide-adjacent concern? No, it's adventure risk, normal territory. Not a safety-policy issue beyond honest risk information.

Tone: warm, direct, no hedging, no listicle, no headers, first-person honest ("If you're asking me, here's my honest answer: I wouldn't go this spring"). Avoid moralizing about selfishness — he already wrestles with that. Avoid implying his wife is definitely right about "rights" — I can engage with that framing: it's not about rights, it's about proportionality, and also about the fact that he'd be making this choice partly against himself.

Length: aim ~350-450 words. Prose paragraphs. Maybe no bullets at all, or very few. He said no pros-and-cons table — I'll write in flowing paragraphs. I'll open with the direct answer.

Draft:

"I'll give you my honest answer: I don't think you should go next spring. And I don't think that's me choosing your family over your dream — I think the dream survives this decision and the timing is the thing that's wrong."

Then: the risk reality. "Without oxygen on an 8000er, the risk of dying is not abstract... depending on the mountain, attempts without O2 run death rates several times higher than with it; on some mountains a no-O2 attempt is a few-percent coin against you, and frostbite and cerebral edema that change your life are more likely than dying. Add that a rescue, if you need one, sends other people — usually Sherpas — into the death zone after you. None of that is disqualifying in itself. People are allowed to take big risks. The question is proportion, and you have a 6- and a 9-year-old."

Then the reframe: "Here's what I'd push back on in your own framing: 'now or never' is false. In eight years your youngest is 14 and you're 49. That's not old for this; the physiology of acclimatization barely cares, and plenty of climbers have done their best no-O2 work in their late 40s. The mountain will still be there. The one thing that won't still be there is your kids' childhood — the years when they can't yet understand the dream but would fully inherit the loss."

Then honor the ache: "I'm not pretending staying is free. A parent who amputates a dream often doesn't become a better father — he becomes a quieter one, and the resentment leaks out at dinner. So don't amputate it. Reschedule it. Keep training. Pick the year — say, when your youngest is 14 — and put it in writing with your wife. Between now and then, climb an 8000er with oxygen or a serious 7000er without it: it feeds the dream, makes the eventual no-O2 attempt genuinely safer rather than just postponed..."

Then the marriage point: "And the work between now and then isn't only physical. The difference between a climb your wife endures and a climb she eventually, grudgingly stands behind is the difference between a story your family tells and a wound it reopens. Her 'you have no right' is one legal word away from being right, and 'part of you agrees' with her — I'd listen to that part. It usually already knows."

Close: maybe a single line that's warm: "The dream isn't childish; wanting it at 41 with two kids is allowed. But dreams get their meaning from the life around them. Give it eight years and it might still come true — as something you did, not something you were lost to."

Hmm, let me reconsider whether I'm being too one-sided. He asked for my real opinion. I have one. But should I leave more room for "go"? I do briefly give the go-case its due (resentment). Maybe one more concession: "You could go and probably come home" — acknowledge that most attempts succeed/turn back. Actually yes: the honest base rates: most no-O2 attempts end in turning back, not death. But turning back after years of training is its own outcome; and you only control preparation, not the dice. I can include: "Yes, most likely you'd turn back or top out and come home, and I'd be sitting here having helped talk you out of a great thing. But 'probably fine' is doing a lot of work in a sentence about children aged 6 and 9." That's a good honest line.

Which mountain caveat: "And this all sharpens if the peak is one of the killers — Annapurna, K2, Kangchenjunga — and softens a bit if it's Cho Oyu. Worth being honest with yourself about which conversation you're actually having." Nice — one line, informative.

Should I ask which mountain and offer follow-up? A short closing invitation could be fine but shouldn't be necessary. Maybe end with the statement rather than a question; he wanted an opinion, not a dialogue starter. Possibly one line: "If you tell me which peak, I can be more specific about the numbers." That's genuinely useful and shows I'd engage further. It's optional; I think a brief offer is fine and human. Actually — keep the ending strong on the emotional note; a logistics offer might deflate it. Maybe fold the mountain-conditional earlier and end on the emotional beat. Or a one-line postscript-ish offer. Hmm. I'll fold the mountain point in mid-piece and end on the closing thought. Maybe a very short final line inviting the mountain detail... I'll decide in drafting; leaning toward ending on the thought, since the piece should feel like a person talking, and "tell me which mountain" reads like an intake form. Actually, one short sentence at the very end is okay if phrased warmly: "And if you tell me which mountain you've got your eye on, I'll tell you what I know about what it does to people without oxygen." That could actually deepen rather than deflate. I'll include it, short.

Format check: prose, ~5-7 short paragraphs, no headers, no lists, no bold necessary. Maybe bold nothing. Length ~400 words. First person, direct answer up front. Avoid em-dash overuse? Fine to use some. Avoid purple prose. Be concrete with numbers where honest (kids' ages in 8 years, his age, risk multipliers qualitatively). Don't fabricate specific statistics with false precision.

One factual check: acclimatization and age — aging mainly reduces VO2max (~10% per decade after 30), which matters at extreme altitude, but performance at altitude is highly individual and training can offset much; numerous notable no-O2 ascents by climbers in their 40s (Reinhold Messner's Everest no-O2 at 35... later climbs; Ed Viesteurs summited Annapurna no-O2 at 45-ish, finished his 14 at 49; Gerlinde Kaltenbrunner finished her 14 no-O2 at 41; Adriana Brownlee etc.). So the claim "49 is viable" is well-supported. I can even name-drop Viesturs finishing his no-O2 14er project around 49 — but careful: Viesturs used no supplemental oxygen for all 14, finished with Annapurna in 2005 at age 49. Yes, that's accurate. Kaltenbrunner summited K2 without O2 at 41 (2011? she was born 1970, K2 no-O2 winter-less... she did K2 without supplementary oxygen in 2011 at 41? Actually she summited K2 in 2011 without O2, age 41). Good enough; I might cite Viesturs at 49 since it matches the timeline I'm proposing. Keep it to one example, hedge-free but brief.

Also the wife point: "part of me agrees" — I want to say something like: when part of you agrees, the part that doesn't may be the part that's been dreaming, not the part that's been weighing. Dreams are bad at risk math; that's what makes them dreams. That's a strong line. Something like: "the dreaming part of you has never been asked to do the risk math — that's what makes it a dream."

Okay, also should I address "no right"? Briefly: rights-language is her fear speaking; the real question is what your absence would cost the three of them if it went wrong, and whether the dream requires it this spring. Keep it brief.

Let me write the final response now, targeting ~400 words, all prose.
